Q1. Limitations of RNNs and the Attention Mechanism
Discuss two major limitations of conventional RNNs when processing long sequences. Explain
how attention addresses them. Encoder hidden states: h1 = [1, 2], h2 = [2, 1], h3 = [3, 2].
Attention weights: αt,1 = 0.2, αt,2 = 0.5, αt,3 = 0.3. (a) Verify normalization. (b) Weighted

Part 1: Limitations of conventional RNNs
An RNN processes a sequence one token at a time, updating a hidden state ht = f(Whhht−1 +
Wxhxt + b). In the classic encoder–decoder (seq2seq) model, the encoder’s last hidden state hT is
the only summary of the whole input passed to the decoder.
Limitation 1 – Fixed-length context bottleneck (long-range dependency problem):
• The entire input sentence, of any length, must be compressed into one fixed-size vector hT .
• For long sentences, information about early tokens is overwritten by later tokens, so the decoder
“forgets” the beginning. Translation quality of basic seq2seq models drops sharply as sentence
length increases.
Limitation 2 – Vanishing and exploding gradients:
• In back-propagation through time, the gradient from step T to step k contains a product of
Jacobians:

• If the norms of these Jacobians are less than 1 the product shrinks exponentially with T − k
(vanishing gradients); if greater than 1 it grows exponentially (exploding gradients). Hence the
network cannot learn dependencies between distant tokens. LSTM/GRU gates reduce but do
not eliminate this.
Additional limitation – Sequential computation: ht depends on ht−1, so time steps cannot
be computed in parallel. Training on long sequences is slow and does not use GPUs efficiently. The
path length between two tokens i and j is O(|i − j|).

Q2. Self-Attention and Scaled Dot-Product Attention
Define self-attention and explain how it captures long-range relationships. Explain the roles
of Q, K, V . Derive scaled dot-product attention and explain the scaling factor. Q = [1, 0],
K1 = [1, 0], K2 = [0, 1], V1 = [2, 1], V2 = [0, 3]. (a) Dot products. (b) Scaled scores with dk = 2.
(c) Softmax weights. (d) Attention output.
Part 1: Self-attention
Definition: Self-attention (intra-attention) is an attention mechanism in which every token of a
sequence attends to every token of the same sequence (including itself), and its new representation
is computed as a weighted sum of the representations of all tokens, with weights given by their
relevance.
Example: in “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired”, self-attention lets the
token “it” give a high weight to “animal”, so the representation of “it” contains information about
what it refers to.
How it captures long-range relationships:
• Every pair of tokens is connected directly: the attention score between positions i and j is
computed in one step regardless of the distance |i − j|. The maximum path length between any
two tokens is O(1), compared with O(n) in an RNN.
• Information is not passed through a chain of hidden states, so it does not fade with distance and
gradients do not vanish along long paths.
• The weights are dynamic: they are computed from the content of the tokens, so the model decides
which words are related for each input (syntax, coreference, semantics).
• All positions are processed in parallel as matrix multiplications, so long sequences are handled
efficiently on GPUs (up to the O(n
2
) cost).

• Value (vj): “What information do I give?” – the actual content that is passed on and mixed

Analogy: information retrieval – a search query is matched against keys (titles) and the contents
(values) of the best-matching items are returned. Separate projections let the same token play
different roles (what it seeks vs. what it offers).

6. Residual connections and Layer Normalization: Help gradient flow through deep stacks

7. Final linear + softmax: Projects decoder output to vocabulary size and gives the probability

Functions of the three sub-layer types:
• Self-attention: Q, K, V all come from the same sequence. Each token gathers information
from all other tokens of its own sequence, building context-aware representations (e.g. resolving
“it” to its noun). In the encoder it is bidirectional; in the decoder it is masked so a position
cannot see future tokens.
• Cross-attention (encoder–decoder attention): Queries come from the decoder; keys and
values come from the encoder output. It lets each target position look at the relevant source
tokens – this is where the alignment between source and target languages is learned in translation.
• Feed-forward network (FFN): Applied to each position separately and identically: FFN(x) =
max(0, xW1 + b1)W2 + b2, with W1 ∈ R
512×2048

2048×512. Attention mixes information
across tokens; the FFN transforms each token’s features non-linearly, adding representational
capacity (and storing much of the model’s knowledge).

2. Different relations in parallel: One head may track syntactic dependencies (subject–verb),
another coreference (“it” → “animal”), another nearby/positional context, another semantic
similarity. A single head must combine all of these into one set of weights.
3. Avoids averaging away information: A single softmax produces one weighted average per
token, which blurs several distinct relations together. With 8 heads, a token can attend strongly
to 8 different positions at once.
4. Same cost: Because dk = dmodel/h, total computation and parameters are about the same as
one head of full dimension 512.
5. Robustness: Redundancy across heads makes the model less dependent on any single attention
pattern; heads also run in parallel.

Q4. Positional Encoding
Why do Transformers need positional encoding, whereas RNNs process tokens sequentially?
How is positional encoding combined with token embeddings? X = [0.2, 0.5, 0.3, 0.1], P =
[0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.3]. Find the resulting representation. Differentiate fixed and learned positional
encodings.
Part 1: Need for positional encoding
RNNs: Process tokens one after another; ht depends on ht−1. The order of the tokens is built into
the computation, so position information is automatically present.
Transformers: Self-attention processes all tokens in parallel and computes softmax(QK⊤/
√
dk)V ,
which treats the input as an unordered set.
• Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: if the input rows are permuted by a permutation
matrix Π, then Attn(ΠX) = Π Attn(X). Each token gets the same output regardless of where
it appears.
• Hence without position information, “The dog bit the man” and “The man bit the dog” give the
same set of token representations, although the meanings are different.
• Positional encoding injects the position of each token into its representation so that word order,
distance and relative position can be used by attention.

(c) How the design captures nearby and distant context
• Nearby context (local attention): Most linguistic dependencies (phrases, adjective–noun,
subject–verb within a clause) are short-range. The sliding window gives every token full attention
to its 2w neighbours, capturing these precisely.
• Growing receptive field through layers: After L stacked layers, information can spread
L × w positions (like stacked CNN filters). With w = 256 and L = 12, the receptive field is
12 × 256 = 3072 tokens on each side.
• Distant context (global attention): Global tokens see the whole sequence and every token
sees them. Any two tokens i and j, however far apart, are connected in at most two steps:
i → g → j. Global tokens act as hubs that collect and broadcast document-level information
(e.g. the question in QA, the topic for classification).
• Task-relevant focus: Choosing task-important tokens as global ensures the most important
long-range relationships (question–answer, [CLS]–document) are modelled directly.
(d) Limitation of the proposed design
Information bottleneck for distant non-global tokens: Two ordinary tokens that are far apart
(beyond the window) cannot attend to each other directly. Their interaction must pass through the
few global tokens or through many layers of local windows, so the relationship may be diluted or
lost. Since the pattern is fixed in advance, it may miss an important long-range dependency (e.g. a
pronoun referring to an entity 2000 tokens earlier) that dense attention would capture directly.

Homework: Attention Mechanism and Transformer – Solutions Page 15
Other limitations: selecting global tokens needs task-specific design; sparse patterns are harder to
implement efficiently on GPUs (need custom kernels); for short sequences the overhead can make
them no faster than dense attention.

Definition: Masked self-attention is self-attention in which each position i is allowed to attend
only to positions j ≤ i (itself and earlier tokens). Attention to future positions j > i is blocked by
adding a mask matrix M before the softmax:

Why future tokens must be masked:
1. Autoregressive factorization: A language model predicts P(x1, . . . , xT ) = QT
t=1 P(xt

The prediction of xt must depend only on earlier tokens.
2. Prevent cheating in training: During training the whole target sentence is input at once
(teacher forcing) for parallel computation. Without the mask, the position predicting xt+1 could
simply attend to xt+1 itself and copy it; the loss would be near zero but the model would learn

3. Train–inference consistency: At inference the future tokens do not exist yet. The mask
makes training conditions identical to generation conditions.
4. Parallel training: The mask lets all T next-token predictions be computed in one forward pass
while keeping each prediction causal.

(b) How an autoregressive Transformer generates a sequence one token at a time
1. Input prompt: Tokenize the prompt, e.g. “The student”, and add positional information.
2. Forward pass: Pass the tokens through the stack of decoder layers (masked self-attention +
FFN). Take the final hidden state of the last position.
3. Next-token distribution: Project it to vocabulary size and apply softmax: P(xt+1 | x≤t) =
softmax(htWvocab).
4. Select a token: by greedy decoding (most probable token), beam search, or sampling (temper￾ature, top-k, top-p). Suppose “is” is chosen.
5. Append and repeat: The chosen token is appended to the input: “The student is”, and steps
2–4 are repeated.
6. Stop: when an end-of-sequence token is generated or a maximum length is reached.

Part 3: Why BERT suits understanding and GPT suits generation
BERT for language understanding:
• Understanding requires the meaning of each word in its full context. Bidirectional attention lets
each token’s representation use both left and right context (e.g. “bank” in “river bank” vs “bank
account” is resolved by words on either side).
• The [CLS] representation summarizes the whole input for classification; token outputs are di￾rectly usable for tagging and span extraction.
• MLM trains exactly this skill: filling in a word using the whole sentence.
• But BERT is not designed to generate: it does not model P(xt
| x<t), and with bidirectional
attention it would see the tokens it is supposed to predict.
GPT for autoregressive generation:
• Generation produces text left-to-right, one token at a time. GPT’s causal mask and next-token
objective exactly match this process: training and inference behave the same way.
• The model gives a full probability distribution over the next token, which can be sampled re￾peatedly to produce fluent, open-ended text of any length.
• At large scale it supports zero/few-shot prompting, so many tasks can be done by generating the
answer as text.
• But for pure understanding tasks, each token’s representation sees only left context, which is less
rich than BERT’s bidirectional representation at the same size.
Part 4: Applications
BERT:
1. Sentiment analysis / text classification – e.g. classifying product reviews as positive
or negative, spam detection (using the [CLS] vector).
2. Extractive question answering and named entity recognition – e.g. finding the
answer span in a passage (SQuAD), tagging names of persons, places and organizations;
also semantic search (Google Search uses BERT to understand queries).
GPT:
1. Conversational chatbots / virtual assistants – e.g. ChatGPT answering questions
and holding dialogue.
2. Content and code generation – e.g. writing emails, stories and summaries; generating
code from natural-language descriptions (GitHub Copilot).

Part 4: Role of positional information and the encoder
Positional information:
• Self-attention is permutation-invariant, so without positions, the 196 patches would be an un￾ordered set – the model could not distinguish an image from a shuffled version of its patches,
and spatial structure (sky above ground, eyes above mouth) would be lost.
• ViT adds learnable position embeddings Epos ∈ R
197×D to the patch tokens. During training
these learn the 2-D layout: embeddings of patches in the same row or column become similar,
and nearby patches have similar embeddings.
• When the image resolution changes at fine-tuning time, the position embeddings are 2-D inter￾polated to the new grid.
Encoder:
• Multi-head self-attention lets every patch attend to every other patch from the first layer, giving
a global receptive field (unlike a CNN, which sees only a local region in early layers). This lets
it relate distant parts of an image (e.g. a dog’s head and tail).
• MLP layers transform the features of each patch; stacked layers build increasingly abstract
features (edges → parts → objects).
• The [CLS] token attends to all patches in every layer, gathering the information needed for
classification; its final state y is passed to the MLP head, and softmax gives the class probabilities.
Training uses cross-entropy loss.
• ViT has weaker built-in image biases (locality, translation equivariance) than CNNs, so it needs
large-scale pre-training (e.g. ImageNet-21k, JFT-300M) to outperform CNNs, after which it
transfers very well.

(e) Why Query comes from the decoder and Key/Value come from the encoder
1. Role of each: The Query represents “what information is needed now”; Keys are used to find
matching information; Values are the information returned.
2. The decoder is the one asking: At each target position, the decoder knows what it has
generated so far and needs to know which source words are relevant to produce the next target
word. So its states form the queries.
3. The encoder holds the answer: The meaning of the source sentence is stored in the encoder
output. Keys (from the encoder) let each source token be matched against the decoder’s query,
and Values (from the encoder) carry the source content that is copied into the decoder.
4. Alignment: The 3 × 5 weight matrix is a soft alignment between target and source words, e.g.
when generating the French word “chat”, the query attends most to the English key “cat”. This
replaces the fixed context vector of RNN seq2seq models (Q1).
